start.text: Hi! I'm Johnny Lago, an Industrial and Systems Engineering student at Rutgers. I love getting hands-on and finding out how things actually work.

choices.label: What do you like about engineering?

curiosity.text: For me, the best part is trying something new. You can learn a lot from a design that doesn't work the first time!

choices.label: How does that relate to ISE?

ise_intro.text: ISE isn't just equations and schedules. We also look at how real processes perform, where they struggle, and what we can do better.

printer.text: This is the Stratasys uPrint SE / SE Plus, an FDM 3D printer. It builds physical parts one layer at a time from heated plastic.

choices.label: What could I build with it?
What makes this useful for students?

fdm.text: FDM stands for Fused Deposition Modeling. The printer deposits thin paths of thermoplastic, building each new layer on the last.

material.text: This system uses ABSplus model material, which can be useful for durable prototypes. The material matters because a part has to do more than look right.

choices.label: What do you mean by “do more”?

example.text: Imagine designing a bracket in CAD. It looks perfect on screen, but when you print it, you discover the holes don't quite line up.

functional.text: A functional prototype lets you check things like fit and handling before committing to a final design. It's a way to test an idea in the real world.

choices.label: How does this help ISE students?

iteration.text: I'd change the design, print another version, and test again. That cycle of building, learning, and improving is what makes this exciting.

choices.label: How is this relevant to ISE?

supports.text: Some designs have overhangs or spaces that can't be printed in midair. The printer can add temporary support material while the part is being made.

choices.label: How do you remove the supports?

cleaning.text: Compatible soluble supports can be removed in a separate cleaning process. There's a support-cleaning machine elsewhere in this room if you want to learn more.

tradeoffs.text: A complicated shape may be possible to print, but it can take more time, material, and cleanup. Engineers have to weigh those tradeoffs.

workflow.text: That's a good reminder that manufacturing doesn't end when the printer stops. Removing supports and checking the finished part are steps in the process, too.

choices.label: How would I improve the process?

design.text: For ISE students, it's a chance to connect design with manufacturing. We can test whether a part works and whether the whole process is efficient and repeatable.

metrics.text: I'd look at build time, material used, fit, failed prints, and how often the process needs rework. Then I'd ask what we could change and test next.

failures.text: A failed print isn't just a setback. It's information: maybe the settings, geometry, support, or material choice needs another look.

takeaway.text: Here's what I'd remember: you don't really know how good a design is until you try it. Be curious, test your ideas, and keep improving them.

choices.label: Can I ask about the supports?

ise_wrap.text: That's the ISE mindset I like: understand the system, ask better questions, and keep looking for ways to make it work better.

finish.text: Thanks for stopping by! Feel free to explore the printers in any order. If you're curious about post-processing, look for the support-cleaning machine too.

early_exit.text: Of course! Enjoy looking around, and come back if you want to keep talking about the uPrint.
